title: The Visitor of Old Chapel Road
premise: Sable Montrose arrives in the village of Hollowmere to appraise Wrenfield House on Old Chapel Road, a property whose previous surveyor vanished in 1979, leaving behind notes that describe the house in the first person. As Sable measures its rooms, she realizes the house is measuring her back, cataloguing her grief, her debts, her twelve years of pretending the noises in her own flat were pipes. The melted church bell rings at dusk, and the villagers—who have all survived by feeding the house a stranger once a generation—reveal she was invited long ago: her grandmother fled Wrenfield in 1911 and the debt passed down. To survive until sunrise, Sable must either let the house take her or do what no Montrose has dared: give it back its own history, reading the vanished surveyor's notes aloud until the house must appraise itself, and it finds the sum wanting. At dawn the house stands empty, and Sable, changed, chooses to stay—not as its victim, but as the one thing it cannot price.
about_author: Lior Ishikawa is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing structurally unsound homes across rural England before turning to horror. They write in converted chapels and claim to have never once slept in a house they haven't personally surveyed.

chapters.title: The Measurement Begins
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She arrives in Hollowmere to appraise Wrenfield House, finding the previous surveyor's 1979 clipboard still hanging by the door, its notes written in a voice that isn't his. The rooms seem slightly larger when unobserved. Emotional beat: professional detachment as armor, already cracking.

chapters.title: Rooms That Breathe
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, second day. Her laser measure returns impossible figures; a hallway is four feet longer at midnight. She finds her own handwriting in the old notes, describing her flat's noises from twelve years ago. Emotional beat: the horror of being known by a place she's never been.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. At dusk the church tower rings, though the bell was melted in 1911. The village shopkeeper, Mrs. Aldery, goes pale and says only: 'It's ringing for someone.' Sable's car won't start; the road out loops back to Old Chapel Road. Emotional beat: escape closing like a trap.

chapters.title: What the Villagers Owe
chapters.summary: Alternating Sable and Mrs. Aldery POV. In the pub, Aldery explains the covenant: every generation the village invites a stranger to Wrenfield, and the house spares them all. Sable's grandmother was the one who got away in 1911—and the house has waited. Emotional beat: belonging revealed as complicity.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Pipes
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, flashback-heavy. She confronts the noises in her old flat—the footsteps, the breathing in the wall—and admits they followed her from a childhood visit to a house she can't fully remember. The house has always been appraising her. Emotional beat: grief and self-deception collapsing.

chapters.title: The Surveyor's Notes
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She deciphers the 1979 surveyor's final entries: he tried to refuse the house and it took him slowly, room by room, his handwriting degrading into the house's own voice. The last line: 'It wants to be read to. It wants to be told what it is.' Emotional beat: dread sharpening into strategy.

chapters.title: Nightfall on Old Chapel Road
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sunset comes early; the doors seal. The house begins walking her through its rooms, showing her the vanished, including her grandmother's unfinished escape—half a shoeprint in the attic dust, preserved for a century. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into terrible intimacy.

chapters.title: The Appraisal of Wrenfield House
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, climax begins. She turns her instruments on the house itself and reads aloud: every crack, every rot beam, every crime soaked into its timber—the fire of 1911, the bell melted to hide a death. The house convulses, forced to hear its own valuation. Emotional beat: defiance as weapon.

chapters.title: The Sum of Its Sins
chapters.summary: Climax. The house fights back with her grandmother's voice, offering her the belonging she's starved for—a home, a history, an end to invisibility. Sable refuses: belonging bought with someone else's price isn't belonging. She finishes the appraisal: the house is worth nothing, owes everything. Emotional beat: the price of survival refused.

chapters.title: Sunrise, and Staying
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, resolution. Dawn finds Wrenfield hollow, its rooms merely rooms, the bell silent. The villagers watch her warily—she broke the covenant and they must find a new arrangement with what remains. Sable signs the deed, moves in, and begins repairs. Emotional beat: belonging chosen, not granted.
